title: Brand identity in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about the names, colours, logos and shapes that make a brand recognisable, and what people actually remember.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are, not just on what you think.

outro.heading: What makes a brand stick?
paras: Logos are cheap or expensive, loved or mocked, but none of that decides whether people remember them.
Today, think about which parts of a brand people really notice.

questions.q: Nike's swoosh was designed in 1971 by Carolyn Davidson, a design student in Portland. What was she paid for it?
questions.explain: $35, for 17.5 hours' work. Phil Knight said he didn't love it but expected it to grow on him. In 1983 Nike gave Davidson a gold swoosh ring and some company shares as thanks.

questions.q: In 2008 Pepsi had its round logo redrawn by the Arnell Group, tilting the white band into a kind of smile. What was the agency reportedly paid?
questions.explain: A reported $1 million, for a design that kept the red, white and blue circle and changed the angle of the white band. A 27-page agency document explaining the new design later leaked and was widely mocked online.

questions.q: Tiffany & Co.'s blue has its own Pantone colour, created in 2001 and called 1837 Blue. What does 1837 refer to?
options: The street number of its first shop
The year the blue box appeared
questions.explain: 1837 is the year Charles Lewis Tiffany and John Young opened their first shop in New York. Tiffany registered the colour as a trade mark in 1998, and Pantone makes 1837 Blue as a private colour, not one in its public range.
questions.source: CNN Style, The story behind Tiffany & Co.'s famous blue

questions.q: Cadbury tried to register its purple (Pantone 2685C) as a trade mark for chocolate. In 2013, after a challenge from Nestlé, what did the Court of Appeal decide?
options: Cadbury owns it only with its name
The application was too vague to register
No colour can ever be a trade mark
questions.explain: The judges said a mark for purple as the 'predominant' colour covered too many possible uses to be registered. Owning a colour in law is hard: it has to be described precisely, and shoppers must link it with one brand.
questions.source: Court of Appeal, Nestlé v Cadbury [2013] EWCA Civ 1174; Confectionery News, October 2013

questions.q: In a 2015 UCLA study, 85 students were asked to draw the Apple logo from memory. How many drew it correctly?
questions.sub: fewer than half could even pick it out
questions.explain: Just one, although most of them used Apple products. Fewer than half could pick the correct logo from a line-up. Seeing a logo every day doesn't mean remembering its details.
questions.source: Blake, Nazarian & Castel, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 2015 (UCLA)

questions.q: Registering a trade mark protects a brand's name or logo across the EU. How many EU trade mark applications did the EU's intellectual property office receive in 2025?
questions.explain: 196,886, up 9.1% on 2024, and with design applications added it was the busiest year in the office's history. German applicants filed 12.7% of them, more than any other EU country; applicants from China filed almost 16%.
questions.source: EUIPO, annual filing figures, January 2026 (via Trademark Lawyer Magazine)

questions.q: A large global study asks people which brands they would really miss. In 2025, what share of brands did it find could disappear without most people caring?
questions.sub: of brands, across the markets surveyed
questions.explain: 78%, up five points on the year before. The Havas study has found similar results for over a decade: most brands are noticed, but few are missed. The ones that are missed tend to make a real difference to people's lives.
questions.source: Havas Group, Meaningful Brands 2025 (via LBB Online, July 2025)

questions.q: In 1915 Coca-Cola asked glassmakers to design a new bottle. What did the brief say it must be?
options: Recognisable by touch in the dark
Strong enough to send by post
questions.explain: A bottle you could recognise by feel in the dark, or even lying broken on the ground. Eight to ten glassmakers took up the challenge, and a design from the Root Glass Company of Indiana was chosen in 1916.
questions.source: The Coca-Cola Company, history of the contour bottle
